summary: For ages 4–6 (Reception/Kindergarten to Year 1): the successor principle — each successive counting number names a quantity exactly ONE larger than the one before, and going back one is one less. The aim is to turn the flat count sequence into a structure of +1 / −1 steps, laying the ground for the number line, counting-on and early addition/subtraction. Teach 'one more' and 'one less' together as inverse moves, link the spoken word-step to an actual quantity-step, and build towards counting-on (finding 'one more than 5' as 6 without restarting at 1).
misconceptions: Recounting from 1 to find 'one more' instead of counting-on (successor not yet linked to cardinality).
Knowing 'one more' but not 'one less' — the backward direction lags because the string is learned forward only.
Treating 'one more' as merely 'the next word I say' rather than a quantity one larger (fails when the count starts wrong).
Not realising every step is exactly one — thinking numbers grow by an inconsistent amount.

activities.title: One more, one less in lockstep
steps: Build a tower with cubes (or fill a ten-frame one cell at a time) and say the count as you go.
Before adding, predict: 'If I add one more cube, what number will it be?' Then add exactly one cube and check that the count moves to the next word.
Add one cube and say the next number in the same beat, so that 'the next number' means 'one more thing'.
Now remove one cube and say the number that is one less, naming it as the mirror move of adding one.
On a number track, hop a marker (or a frog along lily-pads) exactly one place right for 'one more' and one place left for 'one less'.
activities.insight: Each successive counting number is a quantity exactly one larger than the previous one, and one back is exactly one smaller; +1 and −1 are a single step in opposite directions on the same track.

activities.title: Counting on from a hidden total
steps: Count a set of objects into a box or under a cover, then agree on how many are inside (e.g. 7).
With the set hidden, drop in exactly one more and answer, without recounting, how many there are now.
Explain how you knew — 'one more than 7 is the next number, 8' — rather than reopening the box.
Try a chain: 'What's one more than 8? And one more than that?' naming each successor without restarting at 1.
Reverse it: 'If I take one back out, how many now?' to practise the predecessor the same way.
activities.insight: Once you know how many a set has (its cardinality), finding one more is just naming the next counting word — you do not need to recount from one.

activities.title: Reading the staircase and retrieval practice
steps: Study a staircase/number track labelled 1..10 and describe how each step compares to the one before.
Point to where 'one more' and 'one less' live relative to a chosen number.
Answer quick fill-in prompts: 'One more than 6 is ___', 'One less than 6 is ___', and 'What number comes next after 8?'
Contrast a single step (+1) with a two-step jump, noticing that a jump of two is not 'one more' (an early taste of skip counting).
activities.insight: The +1 structure is consistent all along the sequence: every step up is one larger and every step down is one smaller; a fixed staircase can show this structure even though you are not building it yourself.

checkQuestion: This box has 7 marbles inside — I've told you there are 7, but you can't see them. Now I drop in ONE more marble. Without counting, how many marbles are in the box now? How did you know?
checkAnswer: 8 — because one more than 7 is the next counting number, 8. Adding one moves you one step up the count.
